body.text: Cambodia did its best. By hosting the latest installment of the Francophonie summit, authorities proved they could deliver on the pomp and ceremony that came with the celebration of all things French and cater for delegates and heads of state from more than 80 countries.

A 14-year restoration of an 11th-century temple, the West Mebon, was inaugurated by King Norodom Sihamoni and French President Emmanuel Macron, who delighted locals by taking a lengthy stroll through the streets of Phnom Penh and Siem Reap with his wife Brigitte.

Macron also signed 29 bilateral deals with Prime Minister Hun Manet, ranging from defense and health to digital technology and, of course, culture. The biennial International Organization of La Francophonie (OIF) summit could have been such a resounding success.

But behind the fairy lights and fireworks, the fantastic cuisine and wine tastings, were the ghosts and sins of Cambodia’s past. Macron did not shy from these issues, telling a press conference he wanted the assassination of the Khmer-French opposition politician Lim Kimya fully investigated.
“I would like to raise the murder case of Lim Kimya in Bangkok,” Macron told journalists, “I want an investigation to find the truth and bring the perpetrator responsible to justice under the law.”

Lim Kimya was gunned down in broad daylight early last year in a tourist precinct of Bangkok. A Thai national was jailed for the murder but despite two arrest warrants issued in Thailand, his alleged Cambodian accomplices remain at large and are believed to be still in Cambodia.

His killing occurred just as border tensions between Cambodia and Thailand were spiraling toward war, another item on the agenda for dozens of civil rights groups and free speech advocates who have tired of a nine-year crackdown on government critics that has resulted in too many people being jailed for trivial offenses.
That includes Facebook posts regarding the government’s handling of the conflict with Thailand.

Macron and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney laid the groundwork for at least some of those voices to be heard. Activists were told both leaders would raise their issues if they received petitions outlining their complaints through their respective embassies.

Petition they did. Demands included the release of about 100 political prisoners, in particular five Mother Nature environmentalists, and an end to scam compounds and organized crime, which have tarnished Cambodia’s reputation as a tourist and foreign investment destination.

“The Francophonie cannot credibly promote shared prosperity while criminal networks operate with impunity and citizens are denied their democratic rights,” said Mu Sochua – a prominent opposition figure living in exile, noting the OIF’s founding principles: peace, democracy, and human rights.

An end to the crackdown and more civic space for free speech ahead of commune elections in June and national polls in 2028 were on the list of grievances as opposition political advisor Rong Chhun submitted his petitions to the French and Canadian embassies.

His plight is typical of many. He urged Carney to intervene over a Supreme Court judgment handing him a four-year prison term, with three years suspended, and a ban from running for political office for five years, following a conviction for incitement.

Local issues were threatening to overshadow a summit and the ruling elite did not want that when they were simply trying their best to elevate Cambodia’s international standing by assuming the OIF’s rotating chair for the next two years.

Complaints were dismissed as a matter for the courts or as irrelevant for such a gala event. But the OIF is an odd lot, boasting 53 full members with a shared French history like Cambodia, a French colony from 1863 to 1953.
It also includes 32 observer members with seemingly little in common, like Ireland, Argentina, and even Thailand, which was, much like the petitioners, accused of unwanted meddling.

Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow had urged Phnom Penh not to raise their festering border dispute – a flashpoint for the six-month undeclared war – at the summit. Cambodia treated the unwelcome advice as a dare that could not go unchallenged.
A flurry of statements and reports carried by the formidable state-run and government-friendly media machine defended Cambodian territory.

“Territorial boundaries cannot be changed by force,” Hun Manet said, noting Thailand’s occupation of Cambodian territory while preaching the need for both sides to preserve peace and stability along their frontier.
And there was one Thai headline: “Hun Manet blames Thailand for border clashes.”
No one mentioned that those borders were drawn by the French and agreed to by Thailand more than a century ago. That would be unseemly.

But it was a nice deflection at the right time. Petitioners, civil society, and Tom Andrews, the U.N. special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Cambodia, who led calls for the release of more than 100 political prisoners, were all ignored.
Cambodia carried off the 20th OIF with aplomb, at the end of the day, by sitting on the moral high ground overlooking Thailand. It was a crème de la crème performance.
But still Macron is seeking justice for Lim Kimya.
